posts.text: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has opened applications for its 2027 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) , a research programme designed to inspire undergraduate students to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). The programme offers participants the opportunity to gain hands-on research experience, work alongside experienced scientists and researchers, and contribute to projects connected to NIST’s scientific and technological mission. The 2027 programme offers research opportunities at two NIST locations: Gaithersburg, Maryland, and Boulder, Colorado . Students interested in laboratory research, scientific measurement, engineering, advanced technology and other STEM fields can explore the available vacancy announcements and submit their applications through the official USAJOBS recruitment system. For eligible undergraduate students, SURF provides an opportunity to experience professional research in a national scientific institution, develop practical technical skills, and learn from mentors working in specialised research laboratories and offices. About the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) The National Institute of Standards and Technology is a United States government scientific agency that supports innovation, industrial competitiveness and technological advancement. Its work covers areas involving scientific measurement, standards, research and development, and emerging technologies. NIST’s research contributes to advances across a wide range of fields. The institution’s work can have applications in areas such as advanced manufacturing, physical measurement, materials science, information technology, medical technologies and other areas where reliable scientific measurements and technical standards are important. Through its academic programmes, NIST seeks to introduce students to research careers and provide opportunities to learn in a professional scientific environment. The Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship is one of the programmes coordinated through NIST’s academic affairs activities. Its central mission is to encourage undergraduate students to consider future careers in STEM by providing a structured research experience connected to NIST’s mission. What Is the Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF)? The Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship is a summer research programme for eligible undergraduate students enrolled at accredited colleges in the United States. Participants spend a defined period working on research projects with guidance from experienced mentors. Rather than focusing exclusively on classroom learning, the programme gives students an opportunity to experience research in practice. Depending on the placement and research project, participants may work in a laboratory, contribute to technical investigations, assist with experimental work, or engage in other research activities relevant to their assigned team. NIST reports that its summer interns have contributed to work involving MRI technology, medication-related research and other scientific areas. These examples demonstrate the range of potential applications of research conducted at the institution, although the exact project available to each SURF participant will depend on the selected research placement. SURF is intended to help undergraduate students understand what a career in scientific research involves. posts.text: UKUDLA Master’s Scholarships 2027 in South The African German Centre for Sustainable and Resilient Food Systems and Applied Agricultural and Food Data Science (UKUDLA) is inviting applications for its Cohort 3 Master’s Scholarship programme for African candidates seeking to pursue full-time postgraduate studies in South Africa. The scholarship supports academically qualified graduates who want to develop advanced research expertise in applied data science, agricultural systems, food security, and sustainable development. Funded by the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), with funds from Germany’s Federal Foreign Office, the programme provides financial support for eligible students pursuing master’s degrees at two partner institutions: the University of Mpumalanga (UMP) and the University of the Western Cape (UWC). The UKUDLA Master’s Scholarship 2027 is designed for graduates who are interested in applying quantitative and computational methods to real-world problems affecting agriculture, biological systems, environmental sustainability, and food security. Through interdisciplinary research, specialist training, and academic mentorship, the programme aims to prepare a new generation of African researchers and professionals who can contribute to scientific advancement and sustainable food systems across Sub-Saharan Africa. Successful candidates are expected to commence their studies on 1 February 2027. Applications for the African Cohort 3 close on 7 November 2026, making it important for interested candidates to review the eligibility requirements, identify a suitable research topic, secure the support of a potential supervisor, and prepare the required application documents in advance. Overview of the UKUDLA Master’s Scholarship 2027 The UKUDLA Master’s Scholarship provides an opportunity for eligible candidates to undertake full-time postgraduate study and research in fields connected to sustainable food systems and applied agricultural and food data science. Stage 2: Central evaluations (September)
If you advance past Stage 1, you’ll complete additional evaluations before your application is reviewed by mentors. The process differs by track.
For Empirical, Stage 2 has two phases:
Empirical assessments:
You’ll complete one or two standardized assessments evaluating research taste and technical implementation skills.
Stream selection:
If you advance, you’ll apply to and rank the specific research streams you’d like to join.
For all other tracks, you’ll proceed directly to stream selection.
Each track contains multiple streams, each led by one or more mentors with a shared research agenda. When applying to streams, you’ll answer stream-specific questions. These are usually short responses, though some streams may ask for a longer research proposal.
Stage 3: Mentor review (October to early November)
Mentors review applications to their streams and rank the applicants they’d like to work with. Mentors often invite applicants to complete interviews and work tests during this stage.
A final matching process uses both mentor and applicant rankings to determine offers.
Offers (Early to mid-November)
Final offers are sent in early to mid-November. The program begins January 19, 2027.
Frequently Asked Questions
When will I hear about my application status?
We will contact all applicants who get into stage 2 with details on how to use the applicant dashboard, which you can use to check the status of your application.
When will my references be contacted?
We contact references only for select candidates in Stage 2. You'll provide your referees' names when you apply, but they won't receive anything from us unless your application progresses.
What do the assessments involve, and how long will the application take?
Plan to set aside a few hours for the initial application — more if you're applying to several tracks. You can expect two long-form answers (about 200-600 words each) and a 20-minute reasoning test, plus one to three track-specific questions for tracks requiring question responses. The reasoning test covers numerical literacy, probabilistic reasoning, and spatial reasoning; no specialized preparation is needed.
If you advance to the empirical work test, the coding assessment takes 3–5 hours. Stage 3 interviews and work tests from mentors vary by stream.
If I'm not accepted, can I reapply to a future cohort?
Yes, and we encourage it. Applying to a previous cohort doesn't count against you, and we routinely have candidates who are accepted after applying numerous times.

You don't have to decide everything upfront, either. Until applications close, you can edit your submitted application and add more project applications at any time.
While applications are open, your confirmation email includes a personal edit link for updating your answers, replacing your resume, and adding or removing project applications. Editing for the current round has closed.
You'll receive a confirmation email summarizing your answers for each application you submit. If you don't see it after a few minutes, check your spam folder before writing in.
No. Every free-response answer must be written by you, without AI writing, rewriting, or polishing (including Grammarly-style tools and AI translation). Your answers are how mentors understand how you think, and we can and will reject applicants for AI-written answers. You're not graded on prose, so short, rough answers in imperfect English are completely fine. You can still use AI to figure out which projects to apply to, or for high-level feedback on your application.
There is one exception. If a disability makes it impossible or impractical to type your answers yourself and you write with assistive technology (for example, dictating and using AI to clean up the transcript), write to us at
spar@kairos-project.org
and we'll exempt you from this policy. Please also mention it in the “Anything else?” question of your application so our reviewers have the context. The exemption covers getting your words into text, and the ideas in your answers must still be entirely your own.
Applications close at the end of the date shown in the timeline above, Anywhere on Earth. In practice that means you have until noon UTC the following day, so nobody is cut off early by their time zone.
We can't grant individual extensions or accept applications after the round closes. If you miss this round, the next one starts about six months later, and we'd love to see you apply then. Fill out the
expression of interest form
and we'll email you when applications open.
Almost none. SPAR is open to anyone 13 or older, including high school students, and there's no degree requirement. Mentors select whoever can contribute best to their project, so relevant skills and motivation matter much more than your stage of education. Do be aware that the program is highly competitive, and earlier-career applicants are weighed against people with significantly more experience.
If you're under 18, please let us know in the “Anything else?” question of your application. We may need a parent or legal guardian to sign a consent form before you can participate.
Yes. SPAR is fully virtual and our mentees join from all over the world. There's no country or residency requirement. The one caveat is that, as a US organization, we're required to comply with US sanctions laws, which may affect our ability to accept participants from certain sanctioned countries or regions.
If you live in a country under comprehensive sanctions, or you're affected by narrower sanctions in some other way (the US Treasury keeps a
list of active sanctions programs
), please write to us at
(we're happy to confirm your eligibility before you apply), or flag it in the “Anything else?” question of your application.
Flagging it won't count against you in selection. We run sanctions screening on all participants during project matching anyway, so telling us early just means we can sort out your eligibility before you and a mentor invest in a match. If you know about a sanctions issue and don't tell us, we may have to withdraw you mid-program, which is far worse for everyone than sorting it out up front.
The other thing to check is time zones. Some projects ask for a weekly meeting in a particular window, and any such preference is listed on the project page.
Mentees apply to projects that mentors have already proposed, so you don't submit your own project as a mentee. You can still bring your idea, though. Apply to the projects closest to it and make the case in your application, and raise it with the mentor if they get in touch. Project scopes are often flexible, and mentors regularly shape the work around what their mentees are excited about.
If you want to run your own project outright, that's the mentor side of SPAR. Mentor applications open a few weeks before mentee applications, around December for the spring round and around July for the fall round.

LASR Labs
London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs is an AI safety research programme focused on reducing the risk of existential risk from advanced AI. We focus on action-relevant questions tackling concrete threat models.
Express Interest
Our next cohort will run from June to September 2027. Sign up below to be notified for when we open applications.
About LASR
London AI Safety Research Labs is a technical AI Safety research programme focussed on reducing the risk of
loss of control
to advanced AI. We focus on action-relevant questions tackling concrete threat models. Participants work in teams of three to four, supervised by an experienced AI safety researcher, to take a research project from proposal to publication over 13 weeks. Teams work full-time and in person from the
London Initiative for Safe AI
, alongside AI safety organisations and researchers.
Alumni from previous cohorts have gone on to work at UK AISI, Apollo Research, Geodesic Research, OpenAI, Coefficient Giving and more, while others have founded AI safety organisations or pursued independent research.
LASR will also be a good fit for someone hoping to publish: LASR papers have been accepted to top ML venues including NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML workshops. Recent highlights include three NeurIPS 2025 main conference papers, one selected for an oral presentation, and a best paper award at an ICML 2025 workshop.
Programme Details
LASR Labs is a 13 week programme which runs thrice a year. Participants receive an £15,000 stipend to cover living expenses in London, and we will also provide food, office space, and travel.
In week 0, you will learn about and critically evaluate a handful of technical AI safety research projects with support from LASR. Developing an understanding of which projects might be promising is difficult and often takes many years, but is essential for producing useful AI safety work. Week 0 gives you space to develop your research prioritisation skills and learn about different agendas and their respective routes to value. At the end of the week, you will express preferences about projects, and we will match you into teams.
In the remaining 12 weeks, your team will take the project from proposal to publication: designing and running experiments, iterating on results, and writing up an AI safety research paper (as a preprint, workshop paper, or conference paper) with an accompanying blog post. You will meet regularly with your supervisor throughout, and LASR staff support teams on research progress and planning across the programme.
Working from the
means working alongside AI safety researchers and organisations day to day. Throughout the programme we organise talks from leading researchers, a careers fair, and visits to organisations including Google DeepMind and the UK AI Security Institute. Participants regularly attend events at LISA, and past cohorts have found collaborators, mentors, and other opportunities through the space.
Topics and supervisors
Previous LASR groups have published on important areas in AI safety, focused on reducing risks from advanced AI. We’ve had supervisors from Google DeepMind, UK AISI, Anthropic, and top UK universities.
In previous rounds, participants have worked on projects relating to:
AI control and untrusted monitoring
,
data poisoning
interpretability probes
chain-of-thought monitoring and faithfulness
sparse autoencoders
steganographic collusion
, and evaluating
scheming
and
evaluation awareness
in frontier models.
Who should apply?
We are looking for applicants with the following skills:
Technical ability:
Machine learning engineering experience and strong quantitative skills.
Research ability:
Willingness to experiment, iterate, and dive into execution under uncertainty. An ability to develop a theory of change for a project focussed on impact.
Communication skills
: An ability to clearly articulate the outcomes and implications of experiments, coupled with
transparent reasoning
.
For more detail on how we think about and measure technical and research ability, refer to
“tips for empirical alignment research”
by Ethan Perez, which outlines in detail the specific skills valued within an AI safety research environment.
Strong participants have looked like:
An engineer with several years of industry experience building and shipping production systems, who had been following AI safety and wanted to move into research full-time. Now working at the Australian AI Safety Institute.
A chemistry PhD student who had spent years reading and writing about AI safety in his own time, and used LASR to turn that engagement into published technical research. Now working at the Arcadia Alignment Project.
An undergraduate who hadn't yet finished his bachelor's, but had founded the AI safety group at his university and built it into a serious community. Now heading to an internship at Redwood Research.
There are no specific requirements for experience, but we anticipate successful applicants will have done some of these things:
Built something substantial they can point to: a research result, a system or tool, an analysis, an experiment, or a proof, in any field, ML or not.
Experience working with LLMs, whether in research, engineering, or serious self-directed projects.
Taken real steps toward this kind of work on their own initiative, for example self-teaching ML, switching from another field, or starting a research project independently.
Research shows that people from underrepresented groups are more prone to experiencing imposter syndrome and doubting the strength of their candidacy, so we urge you not to exclude yourself prematurely and to submit an application if you're interested in this work.

Astra Fellowship
Astra is Constellation’s flagship fellowship, built to accelerate AI safety research and talent.
As AI advances at unprecedented speed, preparing for its risks is critical. Astra brings exceptional people into the field and connects them with leading mentors and research opportunities.
Complete this expression of interest form to be notified when our next cohort launches!
Register your interest
Astra is a fully funded, 5 month, in-person program at Constellation’s Berkeley research center.
Fellows advance frontier AI safety projects with guidance from expert mentors and dedicated research management and career support from Constellation’s team.
Over 80% of Astra’s first cohort are now working full-time in AI safety roles in organizations such as Redwood Research, METR, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and the UK AI Security Institute. This round, we want to go further: placing even more people into the highest-impact roles, and helping fellows launch new initiatives to tackle urgent but neglected problems.
Trusted by the best
What we're looking for
We’re looking for talented people that are excited to pursue new ideas and projects that advance safe AI. You may be a strong fit if you:
Are motivated to reduce catastrophic risks from advanced AI
Bring technical or domain-specific experience relevant to the focus areas of empirical research and strategy & governance
Would like to transition into a full-time AI safety role or start your own AI safety focused organization
Prior AI safety experience is not required. Many of our most impactful fellows entered from adjacent fields and quickly made significant contributions. If you're interested but not sure you meet every qualification, we’d still encourage you to apply.
Strategy and Governance Stream
For applicants who have strong familiarity with catastrophic risks from AI, are highly agentic, and are capable of working on difficult and unscoped problems.

Fellows will work on machine learning research in core technical safety topics, such as AI alignment, AI control, model evaluations, and scalable oversight.

posts.text: Professionals seeking meaningful career opportunities in education, data analytics, research, monitoring and evaluation, and international development should explore three full-time, permanent positions with EIDU e.V. The organisation is recruiting for a Learning Data Analyst, Head of Research, and Head of Measurement & Evaluation to strengthen its Impact team and help improve educational outcomes for children at scale. These opportunities are designed for professionals who want to use evidence, technology, research, and data-driven decision-making to address one of the world’s most important challenges: ensuring that every child has access to effective foundational education. EIDU works with governments to strengthen public education systems, with a particular focus on literacy and numeracy. Its technology-enabled platform supports learners, teachers, education officers, and ministry staff within national education systems. As the organisation expands its work across countries, it is seeking professionals who can analyse learning data, design and lead rigorous research, and establish reliable systems for measuring programme performance and educational impact. The vacancies offer an opportunity to contribute to an international organisation working at the intersection of education, technology, evidence generation, and public-sector systems strengthening. The organisation partners with governments to strengthen public education systems at scale. Rather than operating only as a standalone education provider, EIDU integrates technology-enabled educational interventions into national systems, supporting the people and institutions responsible for delivering education. Its platform serves multiple groups within the education system, including: Learners , who use educational interventions intended to strengthen foundational learning. Teachers , who are supported in delivering learning activities and improving educational practice. Education officers , who need information to monitor and support implementation.
